implementation_notes: C gets atomics from C11's <stdatomic.h> (atomic_int, atomic_flag, memory_order_relaxed/acquire/release/acq_rel/seq_cst) and from the compiler builtins __atomic_* and __sync_* for older toolchains. The C11 rule to internalise: an atomic operation with relaxed ordering still participates in no happens-before relation, so publishing data with a relaxed store and reading it with a relaxed load is a data race by the standard even though it 'works' on x86. Atomic objects must be declared with the _Atomic qualifier and accessed through atomic_load/atomic_store or the operators; passing a plain int* where an atomic is expected is a type error, which is the language's safety net.
idiom_name: C11 <stdatomic.h> atomic_* with memory_order_*; __atomic_* builtins for pre-C11
pitfalls: memory_order_relaxed on the failure path of a CAS may not be stronger than the success order - the compiler enforces this, so read the diagnostic rather than casting around it.
atomic_flag has only test_and_set and clear (no exchange with a value); use an atomic_bool or a lock-free word for anything more.
The pre-C11 __sync_* builtins are full-barrier only and are deprecated for new code; prefer __atomic_* which allows choosing the order.
A non-atomic access to a variable that is otherwise atomic is a data race by the C11 definition, and the race detector will flag it even though it is invisible on x86.
